extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO OED counsel, and attorneys subject to USPTO discipline proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline proceedings to evaluate practitioner conduct, prove violations of the Disciplinary Rules, and determine appropriate sanctions. Focused on neglect, reasonable inquiry/certification duties, knowledge elements for misconduct, evidentiary and sanctioning considerations under USPTO regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. 37 C.F.R. § 11.49. A Respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All allegations of disciplinary violations must be established by clear and convincing evidence; affirmative defenses also require clear and convincing proof. This affects how evidence is weighed and the level of certainty required for findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory grounds for suspension or exclusion (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the USPTO if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office (35 U.S.C. § 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline can be based on statutory standards of incompetence, disreputability, gross misconduct, or regulatory violations; findings should tie conduct to these statutory grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of a legal matter (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall not neglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.' Neglect is defined as 'the omission of proper attention to a person or thing' (Black's) and, per ABA informal opinion, involves indifference and a consistent failure to carry out obligations or a conscious disregard rather than a single inadvertent error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect generally requires a pattern or course of conduct and a time element; a single inadvertent mistake ordinarily will not constitute neglect. However, failure to monitor a matter (e.g., no functioning docket/suspense system, not following up on expected PTO acknowledgements) so that an error persists can constitute neglect. There is no 'knowing' element in §10.77(c) — neglect can be inadvertent if it demonstrates disregard over time. Example anti-patterns: non-interactive manual filing systems without ticklers, forgetting matters for extended periods, not checking for expected USPTO postcards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry before certifying filings (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.18(b), 11.18(b); violation via 10.23(c)(15))
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing a document submitted to the USPTO, a practitioner certifies that he has conducted 'an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances' to ascertain that 'the claims and other legal contentions therein are warranted by existing law.' Signing without such an inquiry violates the Disciplinary Rules (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable inquiry includes checking statutory bars (e.g., on-sale/publication under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)), prior art/publications, whether the invention was offered for sale or published, and client communications about intervening events. Antipatterns: filing an application without checking that the invention wasn't already published or offered for sale (including on one's own website), or otherwise failing to investigate patentability before certifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge requirement for certain misconduct counts (e.g., 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 10.23(c)(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Disciplinary Rules proscribe 'knowingly' advancing unwarranted claims or 'knowingly' failing to disclose information required by law. Violations of these provisions require proof that the practitioner knew the conduct or information at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For counts that include a 'knowing' element, the OED Director must prove the practitioner's knowledge (or intent). If the practitioner genuinely lacked awareness of the disqualifying facts (e.g., did not know § 102(b) applied), those particular counts are not proven. Distinguish these from rules like §10.77(c) where 'knowledge' is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative defense pleading and proof requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To raise an affirmative defense, a respondent must 'state affirmatively in the answer special matters of defense.' The statement must (1) specify the defense, (2) explain the defense's nexus to the alleged misconduct, and (3) explain why it provides a defense. Affirmative defenses must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bare or generic assertion that the complaint fails to state a claim is insufficient. The defense must be pleaded with factual and legal specificity and supported at hearing with clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated duties to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often consult the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance. Aggravating factors include prior disciplinary history and repeated misconduct; mitigating factors can include restitution, successful career history, or absence of dishonest intent. The practitioner’s experience can be either aggravating (if it suggests awareness of duties) or mitigating (if it demonstrates overall competence). The nature and extent of harm (actual vs speculative) influence the severity of sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior disciplinary history as aggravating factor and reporting obligations (ABA §9.22; 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior discipline may be considered as an aggravating factor in the sanction stage (ABA Standards § 9.22). Practitioners are obligated to inform the OED Director of any public censure, reprimand, probation, suspension, or disbarment in another jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior settled disciplinary results may be admitted to show pattern or to aggravate sanctions but cannot be used to punish for the same conduct already adjudicated. Filing with the OED Director satisfies the reporting obligation; transmitting copies to the adjudicating court is not required by the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevancy and admissibility of evidence of pattern of practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of prior similar representations or prior applications may be relevant and admissible to show a standard pattern of practice, state of mind, or context for conduct; such evidence is not inherently unduly prejudicial if it offers insight into intent or routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be excluded if offered for an improper purpose, but it may be probative to rebut claims of isolated error or to show customary practice (e.g., posting inventions on a website as a business practice). The court will weigh relevance and potential prejudice before admitting such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of § 10.23(b)(6) 'catch-all' provision
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) proscribes 'engag[ing] in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.' The court treats this subsection as a catch-all that should not be applied if alleged misconduct falls squarely within more specific subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alleged conduct fits within §10.23(b)(1)-(b)(5), it should be addressed under those specific subsections rather than under (b)(6). A finding under (b)(6) is inappropriate where a specific prohibition applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docket management and office system obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain reasonable docketing and file-tracking systems to monitor client matters and deadlines. An interactive 'tickler' or suspense system (paper or electronic) that alerts the attorney to approaching or missed deadlines is part of reasonable practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-interactive systems (e.g., passive alphabetical filing, computerized spreadsheets that do not track dates) are insufficient. Attorneys must implement safeguards against foreseeable human error (e.g., interactive calendars, manual tickler cards, reliable docket software). Reliance on a defective backup system or passive listing that requires the attorney to remember to check is an office management failure that can contribute to neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate important USPTO correspondence to clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must timely notify clients of important USPTO communications (e.g., Office Actions, Notices of Abandonment) and explain required responses and options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to transmit Office Actions or Notices of Abandonment, or misrepresenting the need for fees or interviews to deter client response, can constitute grounds for discipline. Charging arbitrary or misleading fees for routine examiner interactions (e.g., implying an in-person interview is required when it is not) and using fees or deadlines to dissuade client engagement are improper practices indicative of concealment or neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between neglect and negligence (and when a single act may be neglect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect (for disciplinary purposes) typically involves indifference or a course of conduct showing disregard; ordinary negligence may be a single careless act. Nonetheless, a single negligent act can amount to neglect if it causes significant adverse consequences (e.g., inadvertent failure to appear leading to dismissal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate: (a) whether conduct reflects a pattern or persistent failure, (b) the time element (extended inaction), and (c) the harm caused. Courts consider whether the error was isolated and inadvertent versus symptomatic of systemic disregard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification and candor obligations regarding filings and statements to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are obligated that submissions to the USPTO be true, accurate, and legally valid; certifying a submission implies the practitioner performed the required inquiry and ensured the statements are warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to perform the warranted inquiry before certifying renders the certification false and may violate 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15). Practitioners should document the inquiry performed to support certifications.
